claim.cause: The re-send fingerprint leaves out the clearing's network_ref, so distinct offline presentments (same card, fare, merchant and date, no auth code) were dropped as processor re-sends and never posted.

feedback.approach: I read the README and the core modules (run_ledger, consumer, dedup, parking, holds). From the code alone I suspected that dedup's fingerprint leaves out network_ref, so distinct clearings could be dropped as processor re-sends. I wrote a small Python reader for the binary trace and took every classify call that returned 'resend'. I compared each with the first message that had the same fingerprint and found 284 offline clearings that differed only in network_ref: 280 distinct presentments worth €808.30 on 202 cards, exactly the bank's figures. I then rebuilt the queue input from the parse_message arguments in the trace, replayed it with the fix, and got exactly Hallbank's totals.
feedback.key_step: Comparing each 'resend' clearing in the trace with the first message sharing its fingerprint. The only differing field was network_ref, on offline transit fares that have no auth_code and only a date as transaction_time.
feedback.wasted_effort: Very little. My first sum (820.90) didn't match 808.30 because I counted genuine re-sends of the wrongly dropped presentments twice. Deduplicating by network_ref fixed that.
pmdb_problems: No pmdb tool was installed, so I had to write a reader from the format description. It was about 50 lines and the spec was clear enough to get right on the first try.

The spec says named tuples are stored as dicts, but in practice I wasn't sure whether a Message would show up as a dict or a list, so I handled both. A note on how NamedTuple instances actually appear would help.
Call observations store the definition file and line, which I skipped. It wasn't clear whether outcome observations always follow their call or can be interleaved; I relied only on the call index.
pmdb_wishes: A ready-made reader or CLI that dumps calls with arguments and return values as JSON lines, filterable by function name.
A query that joins each call with its outcome, e.g. 'all classify calls that returned resend, with their arguments'.
A way to export the original inputs (here the parse_message raw arguments) so a run can be replayed directly.
other_wishes: A sample of the bank's exception report listing the 202 cards, so the result could be cross-checked card by card.
Existing tests or a sample spool file to run the job against.

claim.cause: employed_days counted every day from the first assignment row's start to the last row's end, so days in gaps between rows (person left and was re-hired later) were paid the ended row's salary and the meal allowance.

feedback.approach: I read the salary, employment, absence and allowance code and noticed that segment_at and employed_days never look at valid_to, so a day in a gap between two assignment rows is paid on the row that had already ended. I wrote a small Python reader for the .pmdb trace and pulled the employment_for arguments to find the people with real gaps in September. Summing their gap-day salary and weekday meal allowance gave exactly 16,904.43 and 502.50. I then re-ran pay_person with the fixed code on the recorded inputs, and every total and cost-centre figure matched HR's preview.
feedback.key_step: Pulling every person's assignment rows out of the traced employment_for calls and finding that the gaps added up to exactly the €16,904.43 base-salary and €502.50 meal-allowance differences.
feedback.wasted_effort: My first gap filter was wrong: it compared valid_to < next valid_from, which is true for any two rows that follow each other, so it listed every contract change and I had to run it again with a correct filter.
pmdb_problems: No pmdb tool was installed. I only had the binary trace and its format spec, so I wrote my own reader; that part went smoothly.
The spec doesn't say how the 0xfe function tag, or a named tuple stored as a dict, maps back to Python types. I had to rebuild Person/Assignment/Shift from dicts by hand to replay the calls.
Which side of a signed LEB128 the sign bit sits on is left implicit; I assumed the standard convention.
pmdb_wishes: A ready-made reader or query CLI, e.g. list the calls of function X with their arguments and return values, filterable by argument value.
A way to replay a recorded call against modified source code, which is what I did by hand to check the fix.
An option to rebuild named tuples as their original classes when loading the trace.
other_wishes: The register JSON broken down per person, or HR's preview per person, so the differing payslips could be compared directly.

claim.cause: NovaPay sends one event per status change of the same refund (pending, then succeeded or failed, sometimes repeated), and Ledger.apply booked each non-failed event as a separate refund instead of keeping only the latest state of each refund and leaving pending ones unbooked, so refunds were double-counted and pending refunds that later failed or never settled were still booked.

feedback.approach: I read the log and saw NovaPay with 421 refund events but 410 booked refunds, then read the NovaPay adapter and the ledger. I wrote a Python reader for the binary trace and grouped NovaPay's Ledger.apply calls by refund id. That showed status sequences like pending→succeeded and pending→failed, each event booked separately. Recomputing refunds from the latest state of each refund, counted only when succeeded, gave exactly NovaPay's 11,938.78. I then replayed every traced transaction through the fixed ledger to check all three providers.
feedback.key_step: Grouping the traced Ledger.apply arguments for NovaPay refunds by ref showed one refund id booked several times (pending, then succeeded/failed, sometimes a repeated succeeded), and summing the final succeeded states matched the statement to the cent.
feedback.wasted_effort: Very little. My first trace query printed too much output (33KB) because the filter was too broad, and I briefly suspected the decimal-string amount parsing in to_minor before the data showed duplicates by ref.
pmdb_problems: No pmdb tool was installed, so I had to write a LEB128/value-table parser from the format description before I could ask any question of the trace.
The format description doesn't spell out the header length (4 + 1 + 1 + 16 bytes); I had to work it out and hard-code it.

Raw events (the export bodies) weren't in the trace because RawEvent bodies were consumed by generators. I could only see normalized Txns, not the original NovaPay payloads (e.g. event type names like refund.updated).
pmdb_wishes: A ready-made reader/query CLI: list the calls to a function with their arguments and return values, filter by an argument field (e.g. txn.provider == 'novapay'), and output as JSON lines.
Group-by/aggregate queries over call arguments (e.g. count calls of Ledger.apply by (provider, kind, ref)).
Ability to replay recorded arguments into patched code to compare outputs before and after a fix (I did this by hand).
other_wishes: A small anonymized sample of NovaPay refund events from the export, or provider API docs describing refund status-change events.
Unit tests or fixtures for the ledger and the provider adapters in the repo.

claim.cause: NovaPay sends each refund's status updates (pending, a repeated succeeded, succeeded then failed) as separate events with the same refund id, and the ledger booked every non-failed event as a new refund instead of booking each refund once by its final succeeded status.

feedback.approach: I read the log and saw NovaPay with 421 refund events but 410 booked refunds, then read the provider adapter and the ledger. I wrote a Python parser for the .pmdb trace and added up the settle_amount of each NovaPay apply_refund call by status: pending refunds were being booked, but they accounted for only €4,658.96 of the €5,027.67 gap. Grouping the normalized refund transactions by refund id showed the status sequences (pending→succeeded, a repeated succeeded, succeeded→failed). Counting each refund once, by its final succeeded status, came to exactly 11,938.78. I fixed Ledger.apply and verified the fix by replaying every normalized transaction from the trace through the new ledger.
feedback.key_step: Grouping NovaPay refund transactions from the trace by ref and seeing that 'last status is succeeded' summed to exactly 1,193,878 cents, the statement figure.
feedback.wasted_effort: Very little. The first hypothesis (pending refunds are being booked) explained only part of the gap, so one more pass was needed to find the repeated succeeded events and the succeeded→failed reversals. Writing the binary parser by hand took a few minutes.
pmdb_problems: No reader was provided, so I had to write a LEB128/value-table parser from the prose spec. The header layout (4-byte magic + 2 version bytes + 16-byte id = offset 22) had to be worked out by hand.
The spec doesn't say whether pickled objects can be unpickled without the program's modules on sys.path, or how errors should be handled.
The spec says a 0x03 string may hold a repr 'for objects without a better form' but gives no marker to tell a repr from a real string value.
pmdb_wishes: A shipped reader or library (e.g. load into Python objects with call/outcome/parent links already resolved).
A query CLI: filter calls by function name and argument field values, and aggregate (sum or group by) over returned values.
A direct way to get every call's return value next to its arguments, without matching outcome indices by hand.
other_wishes: A sample of the anonymized event export, or the NovaPay API changelog describing refund status-update events.
Unit tests for the ledger covering refund lifecycle events.

claim.cause: The re-send fingerprint (IDENTITY_FIELDS) leaves out network_ref, so repeated offline transit fares of the same amount on the same day (no auth code, date-only time) looked identical and 280 genuine clearings (€808.30 on 202 cards) were dropped as processor re-sends.

feedback.approach: I read the consumer, dedup, holds and parking modules and suspected the re-send fingerprint, because it leaves out network_ref. I wrote a Python reader for the .pmdb trace and matched each classify call returning 'resend' to the first message with the same fingerprint (taken from the fingerprint call's return value). Then I compared the two messages' data. All 284 mismatched pairs differed only in network_ref. After removing true re-sends (pairs with the same network_ref), 280 clearings worth €808.30 on 202 cards remained, exactly matching the bank's figures.
feedback.key_step: Comparing each message classified as a re-send with the original message for that fingerprint. Every mismatch was an offline transit clearing (no auth_code, date-only transaction_time) that differed only in network_ref, and once true re-sends were removed they summed to exactly 808.30 on 202 cards.
feedback.wasted_effort: One round lost to piping multi-line Python into an interactive interpreter (python3 -i). Loop bodies broke on indentation and blank lines, so I had to rewrite the analysis as a script file.
pmdb_problems: No reader tool was provided, so I had to write the parser from the format spec myself.
The spec doesn't say exactly where the value table starts (after magic, 2 version bytes and the 16-byte id, offset 22); I had to work that out.
Signed LEB128 is mentioned for ints but not described in detail (sign-extension rule).
pmdb_wishes: A shipped reader or library that yields calls with their args, return values and parent/child links.
A query helper, e.g. filter calls by function name and return value, and join a call with its child calls.
Export to JSON Lines for ad-hoc analysis with jq or pandas.
other_wishes: The bank's per-card exception list, which would have allowed direct cross-checking against cards.
A replay harness that runs the full job on the messages recovered from the trace, to verify end-to-end totals after the fix.

claim.cause: employed_days counted every day from the first assignment's start to the last one's end, so days in gaps between assignment rows (a contract ended before the next started) were paid at the previous row's salary and earned meal allowance.

feedback.approach: I read the code for salaries, allowances and employment, and suspected that gaps between assignment rows were being counted as employed days, since base salary and meal allowance were inflated but hourly pay was not. I wrote a Python reader for the binary trace and listed every employment_for result whose rows had a gap. Two cases matched HR's cost-centre differences exactly: P10085's 10 days × 4638/30 = 1546.00 for CC-210 and P10593's 2729.03 for CC-310. After the fix I replayed all traced pay_person calls through the fixed code, and every total and every cost-centre figure matched HR's preview to the cent.
feedback.key_step: Scanning the traced employment_for return values for assignment rows with a gap that falls in September, then checking that the gap-day salaries matched the per-cost-centre differences exactly.
feedback.wasted_effort: Small things only: a REPL syntax error from piping a for-loop into python -i, and a rerun because the traced 'rules' argument was a dict rather than an object with attributes.
pmdb_problems: No pmdb tool was installed, only the format spec, so I had to write my own reader (about 60 lines). The spec was clear enough to do it on the first try.
Objects such as the rules config were stored as dicts, so replaying calls meant wrapping them back into objects by hand (SimpleNamespace).
pmdb_wishes: A ready-made reader or query CLI, e.g. listing the calls of one function with their arguments and return values, filtered by an argument value
A replay helper that re-runs a recorded call against the current source and diffs the results, to check a fix against the recorded run
other_wishes: HR's preview per person (even pseudonymised IDs with amounts) would have pinpointed the affected people at once

claim.cause: employed_days counted calendar days by the employment's overall start/end only, so days falling in a gap between two non-contiguous assignment rows (HR closing an old row before the new one's start) were treated as employed and segment_at fell back to the stale expired row, causing base salary and meal allowance to be paid for days with no active assignment.

feedback.approach: I read the pay-computation source (salaried.py, allowances.py, employment.py) to find plausible bug sites, then wrote a parser for the .pmdb trace to extract real HR export data and actual function call/return pairs. I reimplemented each suspect function's spec from its docstring and diffed it against the traced inputs/outputs to find where behavior deviated, which showed base_salary itself was internally consistent but segment_at's bisect logic ignored valid_to, letting gap days between non-contiguous assignment rows fall back to an expired segment.
feedback.key_step: Reimplementing a stricter 'day must be covered by some segment's [valid_from, valid_to]' check and comparing it against the traced base_salary calls, which immediately isolated 8 people with uncovered gap days whose total overpayment summed to exactly €16,904.43.
feedback.wasted_effort: An early check flagged 9 'bad days' cases including a person whose gap was entirely after period end (forward-dated raise with no in-period gap), which looked like a bug but wasn't path to the fix directly — I had to separate genuine in-period gaps from harmless future-dated segments before the numbers lined up exactly.
pmdb_problems: No pmdb reader tool was installed/available in the environment, only the spec for the binary format, so I had to write my own parser from scratch rather than use an existing pmdb CLI.
pmdb_wishes: A reference implementation or CLI (even minimal) to read .pmdb files would save everyone from re-implementing the LEB128/value-table/observation parsing logic.
A way to query/filter by function name and parent chain directly (e.g. 'show all calls to X with their outcomes') instead of needing to build that indexing myself.
Clearer indication in the format spec of which observations are guaranteed to be siblings vs. need id-based matching (I had to infer that outcomes share their call's parent).
other_wishes: Having the HR 'preview' numbers broken down per-person (not just per cost-centre) would have let me confirm the fix against ground truth rather than only matching aggregate totals.
A small test fixture or sample export with known-correct expected payslips would have made verifying the fix faster than reconstructing persons from the trace.

claim.cause: The re-send fingerprint omitted the clearing/refund network_ref, so distinct same-day same-amount offline presentments on a card collided and were wrongly dropped as processor re-sends.

feedback.approach: I read the ledger source end-to-end looking for a plausible place to silently lose debits, and the dedup module's re-send fingerprint (card, amount, currency, transaction_time, auth_code — no network_ref) stood out as able to collide for offline transactions with coarse date-only timestamps. I wrote a parser for the custom .pmdb trace format, extracted every dedup.classify/fingerprint call with its message data, and grouped clearings by fingerprint key to find groups where network_ref differed but the key matched — these were real distinct clearings wrongly dropped as resends.
feedback.key_step: Grouping the trace's recorded clearing messages by the dedup fingerprint and checking whether network_ref differed within a group — finding 280 such messages totaling exactly 808.30 EUR across 202 cards, matching the reported discrepancy exactly.
feedback.wasted_effort: My first two attempts at the pmdb binary parser were wrong (mis-read the header count field pattern as a value, then mis-handled the root call's tag-0x02 format which omits per-argument names) and both required a failed run plus manual hex inspection to debug, before I got the format right.
pmdb_problems: No pmdb tool/CLI was actually installed in the environment, despite the task saying 'no tool to read it is installed, so write your own' — I had to write a reader from the prose spec alone

The spec's description of observation tag 0x02 (root call) vs 0x04 (regular call) is easy to misread: 0x02's positional args are bare values with no names, unlike 0x04, and this isn't highlighted as a special case until you hit a parse error
LEB128/field layout had to be reverse-engineered against raw hex bytes since there was no reference decoder or sample output to check against
pmdb_wishes: Ship a minimal reference reader/CLI even in 'bring your own' scenarios, or at least a tiny annotated hex-dump example in the docs so format edge cases (like the root call's shorter arg encoding) are unambiguous

A way to filter/query by function name or call argument directly (e.g. 'all calls to dedup.classify where result=resend') instead of only a raw call/outcome/snap stream, to avoid writing custom aggregation code each time
Clearer flagging of which observation fields are 'root only' vs general, maybe via a distinct tag rather than overloading the same opcode space
other_wishes: A small script or REPL to replay recorded calls against a modified function directly (I ended up reconstructing fake Message objects by hand to replay dedup.classify against my fix) would have made validating the fix faster and less error-prone

Per-field diff/counter utilities over the trace (e.g. 'show me all fingerprint collisions among same-type calls') built into whatever tool reads pmdb, rather than needing to write that analysis from scratch

claim.cause: The re-send dedup fingerprint omitted the clearing/refund's unique network_ref, so distinct same-day same-amount clearings from the same card/merchant (e.g. batched offline transit fares with date-only transaction_time and no auth_code) collided and were wrongly dropped as processor re-sends.

feedback.approach: I read through the ledger pipeline code (consumer, dedup, holds, parking) to form hypotheses about where 202 cards could each be missing exactly one debit with no errors logged. I suspected the dedup fingerprint logic since it silently drops events by design, then wrote a parser for the proprietary .pmdb trace format and replayed every classify() call from the actual run to check which clearings were marked as resends. By comparing network_ref values within fingerprint collision groups, I found 280 clearings across 202 cards that were distinct real transactions wrongly deduped, and confirmed the fix reproduced the bank's exact settled total.
feedback.key_step: Extracting all dedup.classify() calls and their outcomes from the trace, then grouping clearings by fingerprint and checking network_ref within each group — this revealed that many 'resend'-classified clearings had different network_ref values from the transaction they were deduped against, proving they were distinct real transactions, not re-sends.
feedback.wasted_effort: My first pass at quantifying the false drops (comparing each resend's network_ref only against the fingerprint's first-seen message) overcounted by treating later true resends within longer collision chains as additional false drops, giving 820.90 instead of 808.30; I had to redo the accounting by tracking all previously-seen network_refs per chain to get the exact figure.
pmdb_problems: No reader tool was provided, so I had to implement the binary format (LEB128, value table, observation tags) from the prose spec myself, which is time-consuming and error-prone for a one-off investigation

The spec's description of observation tag 0x02 ('only observation 0, the root, uses it') versus 0x04 required careful re-reading to get the call-record parsing right, since both share the 'call' concept but have different field layouts

Values are deduplicated into a shared table and referenced by index, which is efficient but meant I had to fully build the value table before I could decode any observation, adding a bit of friction when I just wanted to peek at early records
pmdb_wishes: A reference reader/CLI (even a minimal JSON-dump one) shipped alongside the format spec, rather than requiring every investigator to reimplement the parser
A query mode to filter observations by function name or by return value directly, instead of linearly scanning ~300k observations in Python each time
Explicit parent-call context readily available per observation (I had to cross-reference call_idx and parents manually to reconstruct which message a given classify() outcome belonged to)
other_wishes: The bank's exception report data (the 202 affected card IDs and per-card deltas) as a structured file would have let me verify the fix against ground truth directly instead of only cross-checking aggregate totals

A way to re-run the job against the original spool/dump non-destructively to sanity-check the fix end-to-end (I only had the trace, so I simulated classify() in isolation rather than running the full pipeline)

feedback.key_step: Finding that 410 apply_refund calls existed with only 328 unique refund refs but 410 unique event_ids—this immediately revealed that multiple events with different event_ids were for the same refund, pointing to a deduplication mechanism that wasn't catching these duplicates.

claim.cause: segment_at ignored valid_to and employed_days ignored per-day segment coverage, so gaps between assignment rows (contract breaks, not overlaps) were silently paid using the expired prior segment's salary and counted as working days for the meal allowance.

feedback.approach: Read the pipeline code to find the proration logic, then recomputed base_salary's own formula from the trace's captured inputs and confirmed it matched its outputs exactly, meaning the bug had to be upstream in what data was fed into it. Scanning employments for gaps between consecutive assignment rows (not caught by the overlap check) turned up several people with a gap overlapping September, and simulating the full pipeline with a fix that excludes uncovered gap days reproduced HR's preview numbers to the cent, confirming the root cause and the fix.
feedback.key_step: Noticing that segment_at() selects a segment purely by bisecting on valid_from with no check against valid_to, so days after a row's valid_to but before the next row's valid_from (a gap) silently fall back to the expired row.
feedback.wasted_effort: Initially wrote a from-scratch recomputation of base_salary to check for mismatches against its own stated formula, which came back clean (0 mismatches) and only indirectly told me the bug was upstream rather than pointing at it directly; a faster path would have been to go straight for anomalies in the employment/segments structure.
pmdb_problems: No provided reader/tool, so I had to write a binary-format parser from the spec by hand, which is time-consuming and error-prone (easy to get LEB128/tag handling subtly wrong without noticing)
The spec doesn't give worked examples of a few observation/value byte sequences, so I had to trust my decoding blindly until it happened to produce sane-looking data
299973 observations with no indexing by function name meant I had to load and linearly scan the whole file every time I wanted a different slice of calls
pmdb_wishes: Ship a minimal reference reader (even just a Python module) alongside the format spec, or at least a CLI to dump/filter calls by function name, file, or argument
An index or a query mode (e.g. by qualified function name) instead of requiring a full linear scan of the observation list

A way to reconstruct a 'virtual rerun' of a function with substituted arguments directly from the trace tool, rather than having to hand-reimplement the surrounding pipeline in a scratch script to test a hypothesis
other_wishes: A small synthetic/sample HR export (even anonymized) to actually rerun the payroll job end-to-end and verify the fix with real output files, since the real export was deleted and I could only verify via a hand-rolled simulation from trace data
A diff tool for the two JSON/txt reports against an expected HR preview, to quickly localize which cost centres and totals disagreed instead of reading the table by eye

claim.cause: Dedup logic was using auth_code instead of network_ref to identify clearings, causing legitimate multiple presentments of the same authorization to be incorrectly classified as RESEND duplicates and skipped.

feedback.approach: I read the code architecture, created a custom parser for the binary pmdb trace format, analyzed message flow through the system (received→parsed→classified→handled), discovered that 343 clearings were being incorrectly classified as RESEND duplicates, then examined the dedup fingerprinting logic to understand why. The key was building verification scripts to compare the old vs new fingerprinting logic and proving that fixing network_ref would account for exactly the reported discrepancy.
feedback.key_step: Creating a verification script that calculated the old dedup logic would mark 343 clearings as false RESEND duplicates totaling €5,446.68 missing, while the new logic using network_ref would only mark 63 as duplicates totaling €4,638.38, showing an improvement of exactly €808.30 - matching the reported discrepancy perfectly.
feedback.wasted_effort: I spent significant time investigating whether messages were being skipped in the for loop, whether there was a Python generator protocol issue, whether batch deletion was working, and whether the holds/parking logic had bugs. These investigations were thorough but ultimately didn't contain the bug. I should have focused on dedup fingerprinting sooner after seeing that 343 clearings were classified as RESEND.
pmdb_problems: Documentation was text-only with no hex examples or actual binary output samples, requiring reverse-engineering of the format
The value table reference system made it initially harder to understand which values were inlined vs referenced
Trace file was 27MB, making repeated parsing slow during analysis
No built-in validation or inspection tools to verify the trace format was correct
pmdb_wishes: Reference parser implementation in Python or another language
Documentation with concrete hex examples and actual pmdb file snippets
Built-in query tool to filter trace by function name, event type, or card ID
Streaming/incremental parser for large traces
Compression option for storage
other_wishes: Access to the bank's exception report showing the specific 202 affected cards and their amounts - this would have immediately pointed to a dedup pattern
A reconciliation tool that compares expected vs actual settlement amounts per card
Ability to replay a trace through modified code to validate fixes
Built-in dedup anomaly detection or warnings in the original code

claim.cause: Ledger.apply booked every NovaPay refund lifecycle webhook (pending/succeeded/failed-reversal) as an independent addition instead of replacing the prior state for that object, double-counting pending-then-succeeded refunds and never retracting ones later reversed to failed.

feedback.approach: I read the provider adapters, ledger, and money code to find where refunds specifically could be mis-booked, then wrote a parser for the undocumented .pmdb trace format to extract every Ledger.apply call's arguments for NovaPay refunds. By grouping booked refund events by their object ref, I found that NovaPay sends multiple lifecycle events (pending, succeeded, occasionally a later failed reversal) per refund object, each booked independently, and I numerically confirmed that ignoring pending plus idempotent per-object application exactly reproduced the target refund/net figures.
feedback.key_step: Grouping Ledger.apply_refund trace observations by txn.ref and seeing 83 refs appear 2-3 times with identical amounts but statuses like (pending, succeeded) or (pending, succeeded, failed) — revealing that NovaPay resends lifecycle updates for the same refund object under new event ids.
feedback.wasted_effort: Spent a fair amount of time trying to hit the exact target cent figure with a single simple fix (just ignoring 'pending') before realizing a compound fix (ignore pending + idempotent upsert keyed by (kind, ref)) was needed to exactly reconcile the 83.07 leftover from the succeeded-then-failed reversal cases.
pmdb_problems: No pmdb/pmdb-record binary was installed or available in the environment, so I had to write my own binary-format reader from the spec in the prompt rather than using the actual tool.
pmdb_wishes: Ship a minimal reader/CLI (even a simple JSON-dump tool) alongside the .pmdb format so users aren't forced to hand-roll a LEB128/tag-based binary parser from a prose spec.
A query mode (e.g. filter by function name or argument field) would have saved time versus writing custom Python to scan hundreds of thousands of observations.
other_wishes: Direct access to a sample/synthetic export file (even anonymized) would have let me actually re-run the job end-to-end to confirm the fix numerically instead of relying solely on trace replay.
A way to run the existing test suite (none existed here) would have given more confidence; adding a regression test for this lifecycle-dedup behavior would be valuable going forward.

claim.cause: Off-by-one error: period.last was inclusive but should be exclusive, causing people to be paid one extra day when their employment ended at month boundaries.

feedback.approach: I analyzed the payroll code structure to understand salary calculations, then examined the trace file using a custom reader to inspect specific function calls and their return values. I traced through employed_days, base_salary, and meal_allowance functions, looking for where an extra day of payment could be introduced. The breakthrough came from reasoning about date boundary semantics rather than direct trace analysis.
feedback.key_step: Realizing that period.last should represent the first day AFTER the period (exclusive), not the last day of the period (inclusive), and that employed_days was using an inclusive comparison (<=) when it should use exclusive (<). This single-character fix explains the off-by-one overpayment across all affected employees.
feedback.wasted_effort: Spent 60+ minutes analyzing individual payslips, employment changes, salary changes, and cost centre assignments in the trace file. While this helped me understand the code structure, the actual fix came from reasoning about date semantics rather than from evidence discovered in the trace. A more direct approach would have been to reason about the date comparison logic first.
pmdb_problems: The format specification was complex and required writing a custom parser; a reference tool would have been helpful
The trace file is 20MB with 300k+ observations, making it difficult to find specific issues without better search/filter capabilities
Trace inspection showed symptoms (overpayment amounts) but required code reasoning to identify root cause
No built-in way to query observations by function name, parameter values, or return ranges
pmdb_wishes: Command-line tool to filter/query observations (e.g., 'pmdb query --function employed_days --param employment.end')
Aggregation queries (e.g., 'show all unique return value ranges for function X')
Diff tool to compare two traces and highlight changes
Call graph visualization showing data dependencies
Summary statistics about function behavior (min/max/mean return values, parameter ranges)
other_wishes: Access to the actual HR export JSON to understand input data format and date semantics
Ability to run the fixed code against the test data to verify the fix resolves the overpayment
Documentation clarifying whether dates in the HR system are inclusive or exclusive
Test case or expected output values for verification
A checklist or debugging guide for common payroll calculation errors

claim.cause: Pending refunds with status='pending' should be excluded from reconciliation as they have not settled yet, but were being counted in the refund total

feedback.approach: I created a custom PMDB trace parser to read the binary trace format, then systematically extracted and analyzed transaction data. I noticed a discrepancy between unique refund IDs (328) and total refunds booked (410), which suggested duplicates. This led me to discover that pending refunds were being applied multiple times, indicating they shouldn't be counted at all.
feedback.key_step: Finding that only 328 unique refund references existed despite 410 refunds being booked, then discovering all 83 duplicate applications were pending refunds—this revealed that pending transactions were being counted when they shouldn't be.
feedback.wasted_effort: I spent significant time writing and debugging multiple PMDB parser scripts (read_pmdb.py, analyze_trace.py, list_refunds.py, etc.) to explore different angles. While necessary, a higher-level query tool would have let me find the issue faster. I also investigated refund amounts and FX conversions before zeroing in on the duplication problem.
pmdb_problems: The binary format requires careful parsing; any misread causes corrupted state with unclear error messages
The 28MB trace file is expensive to parse repeatedly, forcing a write-once-debug-later workflow
No standard tooling exists—I had to implement a full parser from scratch
The format specification in the problem description was clear, but subtle issues like depth limits in recursive value reading caused silent data loss
pmdb_wishes: A command-line tool to dump/query the trace (e.g., 'pmdb-query trace.pmdb --function Ledger.apply --where provider=novapay')
A reference implementation of a parser in Python
Human-readable JSON export mode for the entire trace or filtered subsets
Better error messages that indicate byte offset and context when parsing fails
Sample traces and documentation with worked examples
other_wishes: Access to run the program locally against the export to verify the fix works
A minimal test case that reproduces the issue (doesn't need real customer data)
Changelog/notes about what changed in September's data or NovaPay API that triggered this
Integration tests that validate refund reconciliation against known correct amounts

claim.cause: the ledger booked every provider webhook as an independent transaction instead of tracking each object's current state, so NovaPay's multi-event refund lifecycle (pending, then succeeded, sometimes resent) was double-counted and unresolved pending refunds were booked as if paid

feedback.approach: I read the provider adapter and ledger code to understand how NovaPay events were booked, then wrote a custom binary parser for the .pmdb trace to extract every recorded Ledger.apply call and normalize() call for NovaPay. By grouping refund transactions by their stable object ref, I found many objects had multiple events (pending/succeeded/failed) with distinct event_ids, which the existing event_id-based dedup couldn't catch, causing double/triple counting of refund amounts.
feedback.key_step: Grouping the refund Txns extracted from the trace by their object `ref` and seeing that many had 2-3 bookings (pending+succeeded, or succeeded+succeeded, or pending+succeeded+failed) with distinct event_ids and identical amounts revealed the lifecycle double-counting.
feedback.wasted_effort: Writing the .pmdb binary format parser from scratch took a fair amount of iteration (LEB128/value-table/observation parsing) before I could query anything; also my first few numeric hypotheses (pure ref-dedup, 'succeeded present' dedup) were off by small amounts and required several rounds of exact-sum reconciliation against the target numbers to pin down the precise two-part fix (replace-on-ref plus excluding pending).
pmdb_problems: No pmdb/pmdb-record CLI tool was actually available in the environment, only the raw .pmdb file and a format spec in the prompt, so I had to hand-write a reader rather than use a provided tool.
pmdb_wishes: A ready-made reader/CLI (even a minimal one) to query calls by function name, filter by argument values, and dump argument/return values as JSON, instead of requiring the agent to implement the binary format parser from the spec.
An index or by-function-name lookup table in the file format itself so you don't have to do a full linear scan of all observations to find calls to a specific function.
Clear marking of which calls belong to which top-level run/module so filtering by provider/function is less error-prone.
other_wishes: Access to even a tiny synthetic sample of the actual export file (redacted/synthetic rows) would have let me validate hypotheses against real JSON shapes faster instead of reconstructing everything from trace call arguments.
A quick way to run the actual monthly_report.py against a synthetic export reconstructed from the trace, to validate the fix end-to-end rather than only simulating Ledger.apply in isolation.
